This is because the scattering into phonons is really a scattering off of the nucleus plus the inner-shell electrons rather than just the nucleus, so that one can estimate the rate by substituting the atomic mass numbers in Eq. (40) with the number of bound electrons in each atom. The results of this procedure are summarized in Appendix D.

Polar materials are also sensitive to the scenario where the DM is a boson with mass below ∼\sim eV, where the DM could be absorbed into single or multi-phonon excitations. Fig. 13 shows the reach for dark photon DM, for which the absorption rate can be related to the measured optical conductivity of the material. We expect that polar materials could also be sensitive to the absorption of scalar/pseudoscalar DM with a coupling to nucleons and/or electrons, but the absorption rate on optical phonons should be subject to the same destructive interference that we found for scalar-mediated scattering (Sec. IV). This implies that the multiphonon absorption could increase in importance, as compared to the case where a dark photon is absorbed. We reserve this computation for future work as it requires knowledge of anharmonic phonon interactions.

In Tab. 3 we provide a summary of the target materials that so far have been proposed for sub-MeV dark matter scattering and sub-eV dark matter absorption, and their sensitivity to different models. Single element semiconductors such as Ge and Si have a similar phonon spectrum as polar materials and therefore have sensitivity to the same models, with the exception of dark photon mediated scattering. The optical phonons in Ge and Si crystals do not give rise to long-range dipole fields, so dark photon mediated interactions cannot excite a single optical phonon in the long-wavelength limit (multiphonon excitations are still possible, and have been considered for dark photon DM absorption [33]). We conclude that polar materials can test a wide range of models for sub-MeV dark matter, with the added advantage of a directional dependence in the scattering rate for certain materials. That polar materials are readily available and well-understood crystals also makes them an exciting prospect for experimental realization.

Appendix A Phonon eigenmodes

Density functional theory (DFT) [73, 74] is the workhorse of modern computational materials physics [75]. It is an ab initio method which requires only the location of the atoms in a crystal and a potential describing the ions to find solutions to the many-body Schrodinger equation. It is routinely applied to calculate a broad range of chemical and physical properties of materials ranging from electronic and phonon band structures to binding energies and magnetic properties. DFT’s power lies in its versatility in addressing several areas in quantum materials while maintaining chemical and structural specificity that is not possible in tight-binding and other analytical methods. In its most basic form, DFT calculates the total energy of the system under consideration. From this, many related properties – such as forces and response functions – can be calculated by taking derivatives of the total energy and by perturbative methods.

To calculate the phonon eigenmodes, ν\nu, for a particular crystal, we require solutions to the eigenvalue equation:

∑j′𝐃𝐪,j,j′⋅𝐞ν,j′,𝐪=ων,𝐪2​𝐞ν,j,𝐪\sum_{j^{\prime}}{\bf D}_{{\bf q},j,j^{\prime}}\cdot{\bf e}_{\nu,j^{\prime},{\bf q}}=\omega_{\nu,{\bf q}}^{2}{\bf e}_{\nu,j,{\bf q}} (51)

with the dynamical matrix 𝐃𝐪,j,j′{\bf D}_{{\bf q},j,j^{\prime}} given by

𝐃𝐪,j,j′=∑𝐥′𝒱(∈)′,|,↕′,|′mj​mj′​ei​𝐪⋅(𝐫j′0+𝐥′−𝐫j0){\bf D}_{{\bf q},j,j^{\prime}}=\sum_{{\bf l}^{\prime}}\frac{\mathbfcal{V}^{(2)}_{0,j,{\bf l}^{\prime},j^{\prime}}}{\sqrt{m_{j}m_{j^{\prime}}}}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot({\bf r}^{0}_{j^{\prime}}+{\bf l}^{\prime}-{\bf r}^{0}_{j})} (52)

and 𝒱(∈)↕,|,↕′,|′\mathbfcal{V}^{(2)}_{{\bf l},j,{\bf l}^{\prime},j^{\prime}} are the force constants to be calculated, as shown in Section III.

In this work we use the frozen-phonon method to calculate the force constants and the corresponding dynamical matrix. This method displaces each atom in the unit cell and calculates the resulting forces on the other atoms using DFT. From a combination of symmetry-inequivalent displacements, the full force-constant matrix can be built up using DFT calculations. A post-processing software package, phonopy [38], is then used to solve the eigenvalue problem for ων,𝐪\omega_{\nu,{\bf q}} and 𝐞ν,j,𝐪{\bf e}_{\nu,j,{\bf q}}.

A.1 Computational Details for DFT

Our density functional theory calculations were performed with the projector augmented-wave (PAW) method [76] as implemented in the VASP code [44]. All calculations were performed using the Perdew-Becke-Ernzerhof (PBE) parametrization of the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) [77]. The wavefunctions were expanded using plane waves with an energy cutoff of 600 eV, and used a Monkhorst-Pack [78] kk-point sampling mesh of 12x12x4 for 10-atom calculations, 6x6x4 for 30-atom calculations and 4x4x4 for 90-atom (tripled unit cell) calculations. We performed a full relaxation of the lattice constants and internal coordinates of the structure until the forces were converged to 0.01eV/Å. The phonon calculations and modulations of the phonon modes were performed using the frozen-phonon method as implemented in the phonopy [38] software.

A.2 Crystallographic properties of GaAs and Al2O3

GaAs and Al2O3 adopt the zincblende (space group F-43m) and sapphire (space group R-3c) structures respectively, with the conventional unit cells shown. The cubic lattice of GaAs is equivalent in all three crystallographic directions, with all Ga and As atoms in the cell being equivalent. The primitive unit cell in this case is made up of two atoms – one Ga and one As. However, sapphire’s rhombohedral unit cell has inequivalent in-plane and out-of-plane crystal axes. The primitive unit cell of Al2O3 has two copies of five atoms – two Al and three O. These differing Al and O occupy inequivalent symmetry positions in the unit cell and thus have different surrounding chemical environments. Owing to this, the Born effective charges for each of these five atoms can differ since they will have different responses to external perturbations. The calculated Born effective charges for Al2O3 for the inequivalent atoms are

𝐙∗Al(1)=(2.980.034−0.0342.982.951)𝐙∗Al(2)=(2.98−0.0340.0342.982.951)𝐙∗O(1)=(−1.937−0.0860.23−0.086−2.037−0.1330.314−0.181−1.967)𝐙∗O(2)=(−2.087−1.8870.2660.363−1.967)𝐙∗O(3)=(−1.9370.086−0.230.086−2.037−0.133−0.314−0.181−1.967).\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{ll}\mathbf{Z^{*}}_{\text{Al(1)}}=\left(\!\begin{array}[]{ccc}2.98&0.034&\\ -0.034&2.98&\\ &&2.951\end{array}\!\!\right)&\mathbf{Z^{*}}_{\text{Al(2)}}=\left(\!\begin{array}[]{ccc}2.98&-0.034&\\ 0.034&2.98&\\ &&2.951\end{array}\!\!\right)\\ \mathbf{Z^{*}}_{\text{O(1)}}=\left(\!\begin{array}[]{ccc}-1.937&-0.086&0.23\\ -0.086&-2.037&-0.133\\ 0.314&-0.181&-1.967\end{array}\!\!\right)&\mathbf{Z^{*}}_{\text{O(2)}}=\left(\!\begin{array}[]{ccc}-2.087&&\\ &-1.887&0.266\\ &0.363&-1.967\end{array}\!\!\right)\\ \mathbf{Z^{*}}_{\text{O(3)}}=\left(\!\begin{array}[]{ccc}-1.937&0.086&-0.23\\ 0.086&-2.037&-0.133\\ -0.314&-0.181&-1.967\end{array}\!\!\right).\end{array}

Appendix B Fröhlich Hamiltonian

For the derivation of the Fröhlich matrix element we largely follow the discussion in [56, 55]. We start with a regular lattice of NN cells, with each cell containing a point charge QQ at location 𝝉\boldsymbol{\tau} relative to the center of the cell. The Poisson equation for the potential ϕ⁡(𝐫,𝝉)\phi({\bf r},\boldsymbol{\tau}) for this configuration is:

∇⋅ϵ∞⋅∇ϕ(𝐫,τ)=−∑𝐥[Qδ(𝐫−𝝉−𝐥)−QΩ].\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\infty}\cdot\nabla\phi({\bf r},\mathbf{\tau})=-\sum_{{\bf l}}\left[Q\delta({\bf r}-\boldsymbol{\tau}-{\bf l})-\frac{Q}{\Omega}\right]. (68)

with 𝐥{\bf l} the lattice vectors, such that ϕ⁡(𝐫+𝐥,𝝉)=ϕ⁡(𝐫,𝝉)\phi({\bf r}+{\bf l},\boldsymbol{\tau})=\phi({\bf r},\boldsymbol{\tau}). We have included also a background average charge in the unit cell volume Ω\Omega, to ensure that the system is neutral at long distances. ϵ∞\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\infty} is the high frequency dielectric matrix, which describes the (fast) response of the electrons in the presence of the charge displacement. The solution is

ϕ⁡(𝐫,τ)=QN​Ω​∑𝐥∑𝐪∑𝐆≠−𝐪1(𝐪+𝐆)⋅ϵ∞⋅(𝐪+𝐆)​ei⁡(𝐪+𝐆)⋅(−𝐫+𝝉+𝐥)\phi({\bf r},\mathbf{\tau})=\frac{Q}{N\Omega}\sum_{{\bf l}}\sum_{{\bf q}}\sum_{{\bf G}\neq-{\bf q}}\frac{1}{({\bf q}+{\bf G})\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\infty}\cdot({\bf q}+{\bf G})}e^{i({\bf q}+{\bf G})\cdot(-{\bf r}+\boldsymbol{\tau}+{\bf l})} (69)

where N×ΩN\times\Omega is the volume of the entire lattice. The 𝐪{\bf q} form a regular, NN-point discretization of the first Brillouin zone, the 𝐆{\bf G} are the reciprocal lattice vectors, and we have dropped any constant contributions.

We now allow for a dipole 𝐩\mathbf{p} for every atomic displacement in the cell. For each cell, let us denote the equilibrium position for an ion relative to the origin of the primitive cell as 𝐫j0{\bf r}^{0}_{j}, where jj labels atoms in the cell. The potential induced by the displacement of a single ion is defined as ϕdip​(𝐫)=lim𝐮→0ϕ⁡(𝐫,𝐫j0+𝐮j)−ϕ⁡(𝐫,𝐫j0)\phi_{\text{dip}}({\bf r})=\lim_{{{\bf u}}\to 0}\phi({\bf r},{\bf r}^{0}_{j}+{\bf u}_{j})-\phi({\bf r},{\bf r}^{0}_{j}). Placing the dipoles in each cell of the lattice, we find

ϕdip​(𝐫)=iN​Ω​∑𝐥∑j∑𝐪∑𝐆≠−𝐪𝐩𝐥,j⋅(𝐪+𝐆)(𝐪+𝐆)⋅ϵ∞⋅(𝐪+𝐆)​ei⁡(𝐪+𝐆)⋅(−𝐫+𝐫j0+𝐥).\phi_{\text{dip}}({\bf r})=\frac{i}{N\Omega}\sum_{{\bf l}}\sum_{j}\sum_{{\bf q}}\sum_{{\bf G}\neq-{\bf q}}\frac{{\bf p}_{{\bf l},j}\cdot({\bf q}+{\bf G})}{({\bf q}+{\bf G})\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\infty}\cdot({\bf q}+{\bf G})}e^{i({\bf q}+{\bf G})\cdot(-{\bf r}+{\bf r}^{0}_{j}+{\bf l})}. (70)

where 𝐩𝐥,j{\bf p}_{{\bf l},j} is the dipole moment for atom jj in the cell specified by the lattice vector 𝐥{\bf l}. The dipole is given by the displacement of each ion from its equilibrium position in the cell, multiplied by its Born effective charge,

𝐩𝐥,j=\displaystyle\mathbf{p}_{{\bf l},j}= e​𝐙j∗⋅𝐮j,𝐥​(0)\displaystyle e{\bf Z}^{\ast}_{j}\cdot{\bf u}_{j,{\bf l}}(0) (71)
=\displaystyle= e​∑ν∑𝐆≠−𝐪∑𝐪12​N​mj​ων,𝐪​(𝐙j∗⋅𝐞ν,j,𝐪​a^ν,𝐪​ei⁡(𝐪+𝐆)⋅(𝐥+𝐫j0)+h.c.)\displaystyle e\sum_{\nu}\sum_{{\bf G}\neq-{\bf q}}\sum_{{\bf q}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2Nm_{j}\omega_{\nu,{\bf q}}}}\left({\bf Z}^{\ast}_{j}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{\nu,j,{\bf q}}\,\hat{a}_{\nu,{\bf q}}\,e^{i({\bf q}+{\bf G})\cdot({\bf l}+{\bf r}^{0}_{j})}+\text{h.c.}\right) (72)

where we used the displacement operator in (7).

To obtain the Hamiltonian for DM with effective charge e′e^{\prime}, we multiply the potential in (70) with e′e^{\prime}. Using the completeness relation ∑𝐥ei⁡(𝐪−𝐪′)⋅𝐥=N​δ𝐪′,𝐪\sum_{{\bf l}}e^{i({\bf q}-{\bf q}^{\prime})\cdot{\bf l}}=N\delta_{{\bf q}^{\prime},{\bf q}}, we find that for emission of a single phonon,

H=i​e​e′Ω∑j,ν∑𝐆≠−𝐪∑𝐪12​N​mj​ων,𝐪(𝐪+𝐆)⋅𝐙j∗⋅𝐞j,ν,𝐪∗(𝐪+𝐆)⋅ϵ∞⋅(𝐪+𝐆)a^ν,𝐪†e−i(𝐪+𝐆)⋅𝐫+h.cH=\frac{iee^{\prime}}{\Omega}\sum_{j,\nu}\sum_{{\bf G}\neq-{\bf q}}\sum_{\bf q}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2Nm_{j}\omega_{\nu,{\bf q}}}}\frac{({\bf q}+{\bf G})\cdot{\bf Z}^{\ast}_{j}\cdot{\bf e}_{j,\nu,{\bf q}}^{*}}{({\bf q}+{\bf G})\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\infty}\cdot({\bf q}+{\bf G})}\hat{a}_{\nu,{\bf q}}^{\dagger}e^{-i({\bf q}+{\bf G})\cdot{\bf r}}+\text{h.c} (73)

The incoming and outgoing DM states can be modeled by plane waves ⟨𝐩i−(𝐪+𝐆)|\langle{\bf p}_{i}-({\bf q}+{\bf G})| and |𝐩i⟩|{\bf p}_{i}\rangle, such that the transition matrix element ⟨𝐩i−𝐪−𝐆|H|𝐩i⟩\langle{\bf p}_{i}-{\bf q}-{\bf G}|H|{\bf p}_{i}\rangle is

ℳ𝐪+𝐆,ν=i​e​e′Ω​∑j12​N​mj​ων,𝐪​(𝐪+𝐆)⋅𝐙j∗⋅𝐞j,ν,𝐪∗(𝐪+𝐆)⋅ϵ∞⋅(𝐪+𝐆).\mathcal{M}_{{{\bf q}+{\bf G},\nu}}=\frac{iee^{\prime}}{\Omega}\sum_{j}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2Nm_{j}\omega_{\nu,{\bf q}}}}\frac{({\bf q}+{\bf G})\cdot{\bf Z}^{\ast}_{j}\cdot{\bf e}^{*}_{j,\nu,{\bf q}}}{({\bf q}+{\bf G})\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\infty}\cdot({\bf q}+{\bf G})}. (74)

The expression for electronic transitions is identical, except that the appropriate in-medium wave functions must be used instead of plane waves. Since NN is formally infinite, the matrix element in (74) appears to go to zero. However, in Fermi’s golden rule the squared matrix element is always be evaluated as a sum over 𝐪{\bf q}, which diverges as well for N→∞N\rightarrow\infty. We can thus go to continuum limit by taking

∑𝐪|ℳ𝐪+𝐆,ν|2→N​Ω​∫BZd3​𝐪(2​π)3​|ℳ𝐪+𝐆,ν|2\sum_{\bf q}|\mathcal{M}_{{{\bf q}+{\bf G},\nu}}|^{2}\rightarrow N\Omega\int_{\text{BZ}}\!\frac{d^{3}{\bf q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}|\mathcal{M}_{{{\bf q}+{\bf G},\nu}}|^{2} (75)

where the integral runs over the Brillouin zone. Since we work in the continuum limit for the calculations in Sec. III, it is convenient to absorb the N​Ω\sqrt{N\Omega} factor directly into the matrix element, which then becomes

ℳ𝐪+𝐆,ν=i​e​e′​∑j12​Ω​mj​ων,𝐪​(𝐪+𝐆)⋅𝐙j∗⋅𝐞j,ν,𝐪∗(𝐪+𝐆)⋅ϵ∞⋅(𝐪+𝐆)\mathcal{M}_{{{\bf q}+{\bf G},\nu}}=iee^{\prime}\sum_{j}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\Omega m_{j}\omega_{\nu,{\bf q}}}}\frac{({\bf q}+{\bf G})\cdot{\bf Z}^{\ast}_{j}\cdot{\bf e}^{*}_{j,\nu,{\bf q}}}{({\bf q}+{\bf G})\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\infty}\cdot({\bf q}+{\bf G})} (76)

which manifestly independent of the number of cells in the lattice.

In the isotropic, long-wavelength limit we can drop the dependence on the reciprocal lattice vectors 𝐆{\bf G}. Taking a 2-atom unit cell such as for GaAs, the expression reduces to

ℳ𝐪iso≈i​e​e′ϵ∞​|Z∗|2​Ω​μ​ωL​O​1|𝐪|\mathcal{M}^{\text{iso}}_{{{\bf q}}}\approx i\frac{ee^{\prime}}{\epsilon_{\infty}}\frac{|Z^{\ast}|}{\sqrt{2\Omega\mu\omega_{LO}}}\frac{1}{|{\bf q}|} (77)

where ωL​O\omega_{LO} is the frequency of the optical phonon and μ≡(1/m1+1/m2)−1\mu\equiv(1/m_{1}+1/m_{2})^{-1} is the reduced mass. Here we used that the eigenvectors are normalized within the unit cell (see condition above Eq. 9), so |𝐞j|=1/2|{\bf e}_{j}|=1/\sqrt{2} for a 2-atom unit cell, and that 1μ≈12​(1m1+1m2)\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}}\approx\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{m_{1}}}+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{m_{2}}}), which is valid if m1+m2≫|m1−m2|m_{1}+m_{2}\gg|m_{1}-m_{2}|. With the identity

e​Z∗=[Ω​μ​(1ϵ∞−1ϵ0)]1/2​ϵ∞​ωL​OeZ^{\ast}=\Bigg[\Omega\mu\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon_{\infty}}-\frac{1}{\epsilon_{0}}\right)\Bigg]^{1/2}\epsilon_{\infty}\omega_{LO} (78)

(77) then reproduces Eq. (32).

It now only remains to derive (78). Following Ref. [55], we consider a harmonic oscillator with reduced mass μ\mu, charge Z∗Z^{\ast}, and natural oscillation frequency ωT​O\omega_{TO} (this will be identified as the frequency of the TO modes, hence the notation). When the oscillator is driven by an electric field with amplitude 𝐄0{\bf E}_{0} and frequency ω\omega, the amplitude of the oscillations is given by

𝐮0=e​Z∗​𝐄0μ⁡(ωT​O2−ω2).\mathbf{u}_{0}=\frac{eZ^{\ast}\mathbf{E}_{0}}{\mu(\omega_{TO}^{2}-\omega^{2})}. (79)

The macroscopic polarization vector is 𝐏=e​Z∗​𝐮0/Ω{\bf P}=eZ^{*}{\bf u}_{0}/\Omega, where the 1/Ω1/\Omega is merely the number density of the oscillators. The displacement vector of the system is then

𝐃=ϵ∞​𝐄+𝐏=ϵ​𝐄{\bf D}=\epsilon_{\infty}{\bf E}+{\bf P}=\epsilon{\bf E} (80)

with the frequency dependent dielectric function:

ϵ⁡(ω)=ϵ∞+e2​Z∗2μ​Ω​(ωT​O2−ω2).\epsilon(\omega)=\epsilon_{\infty}+\frac{e^{2}Z^{\ast 2}}{\mu\Omega(\omega_{TO}^{2}-\omega^{2})}. (81)

The ϵ∞\epsilon_{\infty} term is again the contribution from the valence electrons, while the second term is the contribution from the oscillators. At high frequencies the ions are too slow to respond and only the electron contribution remains. Gauss’ law demands that 𝐤⋅𝐃=0{\bf k}\cdot{\bf D}=0, which is trivially satisfied for the transverse modes. For the longitudinal mode 𝐤|𝐄{\bf k}\parallel{\bf E}, this requires that ϵ⁡(ω)=0\epsilon(\omega)=0, which is satisfied at the frequency ω=ωL​O\omega=\omega_{LO} with

ωL​O2=ωT​O2+e2​Z∗2ϵ∞​μ​Ω\omega_{LO}^{2}=\omega_{TO}^{2}+\frac{e^{2}Z^{\ast 2}}{\epsilon_{\infty}\mu\Omega} (82)

One may interpret the additional term as the self-energy correction to the LO mode from the back-reaction of its induced electric field. Combining (81) and (82) yields the Lyddane-Sachs-Teller relation

ϵ0ϵ∞=ωL​O2ωT​O2,\frac{\epsilon_{0}}{\epsilon_{\infty}}=\frac{\omega_{LO}^{2}}{\omega_{TO}^{2}}, (83)

with ϵ0≡ϵ⁡(0)\epsilon_{0}\equiv\epsilon(0). Combining this with (82) results in (78).

Appendix C Nucleon-scattering structure factor

In this Appendix, we present the derivation of the dynamic structure factor for DM scattering in a lattice at zero temperature. We follow closely the discussion presented in Ref. [45], which reviews scattering of cold neutrons in a lattice. To compute the structure factor for hard sphere scattering, we treat the crystal as a regular, periodic lattice with NN cells and nn atoms in a unit cell, for a total of N×nN\times n atoms in the lattice. Summing the potential of the individual scattering centers gives the total potential

𝒱⁡(𝐫)=∑J=1N×n𝒱J​(𝐫J−𝐫)=2​π​bXmX​∑J=1N×nAJ​δ​(𝐫J−𝐫)\mathcal{V}({\bf r})=\sum_{J=1}^{N\times n}\mathcal{V}_{J}({\bf r}_{J}-{\bf r})=\frac{2\pi b_{X}}{m_{X}}\sum_{J=1}^{N\times n}A_{J}\delta({\bf r}_{J}-{\bf r}) (84)

where JJ sums over all the atoms in the lattice, bXb_{X} is the DM-nucleon scattering length, and AJA_{J} is the mass number of the nucleus JJ. In Fourier space, the potential is

𝒱⁡(𝐪)=2​π​bXmX​∑JN×nAJ​ei​𝐪⋅𝐫J.\mathcal{V}({\bf q})=\frac{2\pi b_{X}}{m_{X}}\sum_{J}^{N\times n}A_{J}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}_{J}}. (85)

We then define the structure function by

S⁡(𝐪,ω)≡1N​∑λi,λfp⁡(λi)​|∑JN×nAJ​⟨λf|ei​𝐪⋅𝐫J|λi⟩|2​δ​(Eλf−Eλi−ω)S({\bf q},\omega)\equiv\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\lambda_{i},\lambda_{f}}p(\lambda_{i})\left|\sum_{J}^{N\times n}A_{J}\langle\lambda_{f}|e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}_{J}}|\lambda_{i}\rangle\right|^{2}\delta(E_{\lambda_{f}}-E_{\lambda_{i}}-\omega) (86)

with λi,f\lambda_{i,f} the initial and final states, and p⁡(λi)p(\lambda_{i}) is the thermal distribution over the initial states. Since we envision a very cold target, we only consider the ground state in the sum of the initial states, setting λi=λ0\lambda_{i}=\lambda_{0}. We have normalized S⁡(𝐪,ω)S({\bf q},\omega) such that it is an intrinsic quantity under N→∞N\rightarrow\infty. With this definition, the rate from Fermi’s golden rule is

Γ=(2​π)​(2​π​bXmX)2​1Ω​∫BZd3​𝐪(2​π)3​S​(𝐪,ω)\Gamma=(2\pi)\left(\frac{2\pi b_{X}}{m_{X}}\right)^{2}\frac{1}{\Omega}\int_{\text{BZ}}\!\frac{d^{3}{\bf q}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,S({\bf q},\omega) (87)

where we treated the incoming and outgoing DM particle as plane waves. The integral is over the Brillouin zone and Ω\Omega is the volume of the primitive unit cell.

To compute the structure function, first we note that the squared matrix element in (86) can be rewritten as a single correlation function as follows:

|∑JN×nAJ⟨\displaystyle\Bigg|\sum_{J}^{N\times n}A_{J}\langle λf​|ei​𝐪⋅𝐫J​|λ0⟩|2​δ​(Eλf−Eλ0−ω)\displaystyle\lambda_{f}|e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}_{J}}|\lambda_{0}\rangle\Bigg|^{2}\delta(E_{\lambda_{f}}-E_{\lambda_{0}}-\omega) (88)
=∑J,J′AJAJ′⟨λf|ei​𝐪⋅𝐫J|λ0⟩⟨λ0|e−i𝐪⋅𝐫J′|λf⟩δ(Eλf−Eλ0−ω)\displaystyle=\sum_{J,J^{\prime}}A_{J}A_{J^{\prime}}\langle\lambda_{f}|e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}_{J}}|\lambda_{0}\rangle\langle\lambda_{0}|e^{-i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}_{J^{\prime}}}|\lambda_{f}\rangle\delta(E_{\lambda_{f}}-E_{\lambda_{0}}-\omega) (89)
=12​π∑J,J′AJAJ′∫−∞+∞dt⟨λ0|e−i𝐪⋅𝐫J′|λf⟩⟨λf|ei​Eλf​tei​𝐪⋅𝐫Je−i​Eλ0​t|λ0⟩e−i​ω​t\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{J,J^{\prime}}A_{J}A_{J^{\prime}}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\!\!\!\!\!\!dt\,\langle\lambda_{0}|e^{-i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}_{J^{\prime}}}|\lambda_{f}\rangle\langle\lambda_{f}|e^{iE_{\lambda_{f}}t}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}_{J}}e^{-iE_{\lambda_{0}}t}|\lambda_{0}\rangle e^{-i\omega t} (90)
Since λ0,f\lambda_{0,f} are eigenstates of the Hamiltonian, we can replace the Eλ0,λfE_{\lambda_{0},\lambda_{f}} with the operator 𝐇{\bf H}:
=12​π∑J,J′AJAJ′∫−∞+∞dt⟨λ0|e−i𝐪⋅𝐫J′|λf⟩⟨λf|ei​𝐇​tei​𝐪⋅𝐫Je−i​𝐇​t|λ0⟩e−i​ω​t\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{J,J^{\prime}}A_{J}A_{J^{\prime}}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\!\!\!\!\!\!dt\,\langle\lambda_{0}|e^{-i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}_{J^{\prime}}}|\lambda_{f}\rangle\langle\lambda_{f}|e^{i\mathbf{H}t}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}_{J}}e^{-i\mathbf{H}t}|\lambda_{0}\rangle e^{-i\omega t} (91)
=12​π∑J,J′AJAJ′∫−∞+∞dt⟨λ0|e−i𝐪⋅𝐫J′(0)|λf⟩⟨λf|ei​𝐪⋅𝐫J​(t)|λ0⟩e−i​ω​t\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{J,J^{\prime}}A_{J}A_{J^{\prime}}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\!\!\!\!\!\!dt\,\langle\lambda_{0}|e^{-i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}_{J^{\prime}}(0)}|\lambda_{f}\rangle\langle\lambda_{f}|e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}_{J}(t)}|\lambda_{0}\rangle e^{-i\omega t} (92)

In the last step we used the quantum evolution operator on the phase factor, and made the time dependence of the 𝐫J{\bf r}_{J} explicit. By applying the sum over the final states from (86), we can use the completeness of the |λf⟩|\lambda_{f}\rangle states to obtain

S(𝐪,ω)=12​π​N∑J,J′AJAJ′∫−∞+∞dt⟨λ0|e−i𝐪⋅𝐫J′(0)ei​𝐪⋅𝐫J​(t)|λ0⟩e−i​ω​t.S({\bf q},\omega)=\frac{1}{2\pi N}\sum_{J,J^{\prime}}A_{J}A_{J^{\prime}}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\!\!\!\!\!\!dt\,\langle\lambda_{0}|e^{-i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}_{J^{\prime}}(0)}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}_{J}(t)}|\lambda_{0}\rangle e^{-i\omega t}. (93)

In what follows we will drop the |λ0⟩|\lambda_{0}\rangle to facilitate the notation and all expectation values are understood to be with respect to the ground state.

To compute this two-point correlation function, we write the position vectors in terms of the atomic displacements 𝐮{\bf u} relative to their equilibrium position,

𝐮j,𝐥​(t)≡𝐫J​(t)−𝐫j0−𝐥{\bf u}_{j,{\bf l}}(t)\equiv{\bf r}_{J}(t)-{\bf r}_{j}^{0}-{\bf l} (94)

where now 𝐥{\bf l} labels the lattice vector for a given primitive cell, and 𝐫j0{\bf r}_{j}^{0} are the equilibrium positions of the atoms relative to the origin of the primitive cell. We thus replace the sum over all atoms in lattice (labelled by JJ) with a sum over all lattice vectors 𝐥{\bf l} and atoms in a single primitive cell (labelled by jj). Since the mass numbers AJA_{J} are identical within each cell, we can also take AJ→AjA_{J}\to A_{j}. Inserting this in the correlation function,

⟨e−i𝐪⋅𝐫J′(0)ei​𝐪⋅𝐫J​(t)⟩=ei​𝐪⋅(𝐫j0−𝐫j′0)ei​𝐪⋅(𝐥−𝐥′)⟨e−i𝐪⋅𝐮j′,𝐥′(0)ei​𝐪⋅𝐮j,𝐥​(t)⟩.\displaystyle\langle e^{-i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}_{J^{\prime}}(0)}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf r}_{J}(t)}\rangle=e^{i{\bf q}\cdot({\bf r}^{0}_{j}-{\bf r}^{0}_{j^{\prime}})}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot({\bf l}-{\bf l}^{\prime})}\langle e^{-i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j^{\prime},{\bf l}^{\prime}}(0)}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j,{\bf l}}(t)}\rangle. (95)

We wish to expand this in the displacements, and keep only the leading correlation function. We can do so by applying the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff identity and truncate at leading order. Concretely, for two operators 𝐀=i​𝐪⋅𝐮j,𝐥\mathbf{A}=i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j,{\bf l}} and 𝐁=−i𝐪⋅𝐮j′,𝐥′\mathbf{B}=-i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j^{\prime},{\bf l}^{\prime}} we have

e𝐀​e𝐁≈e𝐀+𝐁+12​[𝐀,𝐁].e^{\mathbf{A}}e^{\mathbf{B}}\approx e^{\mathbf{A}+{\mathbf{B}}+\frac{1}{2}[\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}]}. (96)

Since we are in the small displacement (harmonic) approximation, the operators 𝐮j,𝐥{\bf u}_{j,{\bf l}} can be written as a linear combination of creation and annihilation operators. The commutator in (96) is therefore proportional to the identity operator and we can pull it outside of the expectation value:

⟨e𝐀​e𝐁⟩\displaystyle\left\langle e^{\mathbf{A}}e^{\mathbf{B}}\right\rangle ≈⟨e𝐀+𝐁+12​[𝐀,𝐁]⟩\displaystyle\approx\left\langle e^{\mathbf{A}+{\mathbf{B}}+\frac{1}{2}[\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}]}\right\rangle (97)
=e12​[𝐀,𝐁]​⟨e𝐀+𝐁⟩\displaystyle=e^{\frac{1}{2}[\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}]}\left\langle e^{\mathbf{A}+{\mathbf{B}}}\right\rangle (98)
Next we use the Bloch identity, ⟨eA⟩=e12​⟨A2⟩\langle e^{A}\rangle=e^{\frac{1}{2}\langle A^{2}\rangle}, which only applies to linear combinations of creation and annihilation operators,
=e12​[𝐀,𝐁]​e12​⟨(𝐀+𝐁)2⟩\displaystyle=e^{\frac{1}{2}[\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}]}e^{\frac{1}{2}\langle(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B})^{2}\rangle} (99)
=e12​⟨𝐀2+𝐁2+2​𝐀𝐁⟩.\displaystyle=e^{\frac{1}{2}\langle\mathbf{A}^{2}+\mathbf{B}^{2}+2\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\rangle}. (100)

In the last step we brought commutator back into the expectation value, again using that it is proportional to the identity as long as 𝐀\mathbf{A} and 𝐁\mathbf{B} are linear combinations of creation and annihilation operators.

Applying the above formula to (95), we find

⟨e−i𝐪⋅𝐮j′,𝐥′(0)ei​𝐪⋅𝐮j,𝐥​(t)⟩\displaystyle\langle e^{-i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j^{\prime},{\bf l}^{\prime}}(0)}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j,{\bf l}}(t)}\rangle =e−12​⟨(𝐪⋅𝐮j′,𝐥′)2⟩​e−12​⟨(𝐪⋅𝐮j,𝐥)2⟩​e⟨𝐪⋅𝐮j′,𝐥′​(0)​𝐪⋅𝐮j,𝐥​(t)⟩\displaystyle=e^{-\frac{1}{2}\langle({\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j^{\prime},{\bf l}^{\prime}})^{2}\rangle}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\langle({\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j,{\bf l}})^{2}\rangle}e^{\langle{\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j^{\prime},{\bf l}^{\prime}}(0){\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j,{\bf l}}(t)\rangle} (101)
≈e−12​⟨(𝐪⋅𝐮j′,𝐥′)2⟩​e−12​⟨(𝐪⋅𝐮j,𝐥)2⟩​⟨𝐪⋅𝐮j′,𝐥′​(0)​𝐪⋅𝐮j,𝐥​(t)⟩.\displaystyle\approx e^{-\frac{1}{2}\langle({\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j^{\prime},{\bf l}^{\prime}})^{2}\rangle}e^{-\frac{1}{2}\langle({\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j,{\bf l}})^{2}\rangle}\langle{\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j^{\prime},{\bf l}^{\prime}}(0){\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j,{\bf l}}(t)\rangle. (102)

where in the second line we expand the exponential to leading order and drop the constant piece that does not contribute to scattering. The two exponentials in front are the Debye-Waller factors, defined by

Wj​(𝐪)≡12​⟨(𝐪⋅𝐮j)2⟩.W_{j}({\bf q})\equiv\frac{1}{2}\langle({\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j})^{2}\rangle. (103)

where we dropped the 𝐥{\bf l} index due to translation invariance over the lattice vectors. From (103), we see that the Debye-Waller factor measures the average motion of atom jj relative to the momentum transfer.

Putting the above results together, the structure function is then

S⁡(𝐪,ω)=12​π​N​∑j,j′,𝐥,𝐥′Aj​Aj′​ei​𝐪⋅(𝐫j0−𝐫j′0)​ei​𝐪⋅(𝐥−𝐥′)​e−Wj​(𝐪)​e−Wj′​(𝐪)​∫−∞+∞d​t​⟨𝐪⋅𝐮j′,𝐥′​(0)​𝐪⋅𝐮j,𝐥​(t)⟩​e−i​ω​t.S({\bf q},\omega)=\frac{1}{2\pi N}\sum_{j,j^{\prime},{\bf l},{\bf l}^{\prime}}A_{j}A_{j^{\prime}}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot({\bf r}^{0}_{j}-{\bf r}^{0}_{j^{\prime}})}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot({\bf l}-{\bf l}^{\prime})}e^{-W_{j}({\bf q})}e^{-W_{j^{\prime}}({\bf q})}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\!\!\!\!\!\!dt\,\langle{\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j^{\prime},{\bf l}^{\prime}}(0){\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j,{\bf l}}(t)\rangle e^{-i\omega t}. (104)

To further simplify the sums, one can use the invariance of the two point function under lattice translations, which permits the replacement ∑𝐥,𝐥′ei​𝐪⋅(𝐥−𝐥′)→N​∑𝐥ei​𝐪⋅𝐥\sum_{\mathbf{l},\mathbf{l}^{\prime}}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot(\mathbf{l}-\mathbf{l}^{\prime})}\to N\sum_{\mathbf{l}}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot\mathbf{l}}:

S⁡(𝐪,ω)=12​π​∑j,j′,𝐥Aj​Aj′​ei​𝐪⋅(𝐫j0−𝐫j′0)​ei​𝐪⋅𝐥​e−Wj​(𝐪)​e−Wj′​(𝐪)​∫−∞+∞d​t​⟨𝐪⋅𝐮j′,0​(0)​𝐪⋅𝐮j,𝐥​(t)⟩​e−i​ω​t.S({\bf q},\omega)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{j,j^{\prime},{\bf l}}A_{j}A_{j^{\prime}}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot({\bf r}^{0}_{j}-{\bf r}^{0}_{j^{\prime}})}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot\mathbf{l}}e^{-W_{j}({\bf q})}e^{-W_{j^{\prime}}({\bf q})}\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\!\!\!\!\!\!dt\,\langle{\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j^{\prime},0}(0){\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j,{\bf l}}(t)\rangle e^{-i\omega t}. (105)

It remains to compute the correlation function and the Debye-Waller functions in terms of the phonon eigenvectors and dispersion relations. To this end, we decompose the displacement operators in creation and annihilation operators, as in (7)

𝐮j,𝐥(t)=∑ν3​n∑𝐤12​N​mj​ων,𝐤(𝐞ν,j,𝐤a^ν,𝐤ei​𝐤⋅(𝐥+𝐫j0)−i​ων,𝐤​t+𝐞ν,j,𝐤∗a^ν,𝐤†e−i𝐤⋅(𝐥+𝐫0j)+iων,𝐤t)\displaystyle{\bf u}_{j,{\bf l}}(t)=\sum_{\nu}^{3n}\sum_{{\bf k}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{2Nm_{j}\omega_{\nu,{\bf k}}}}\left(\mathbf{e}_{\nu,j,{\bf k}}\hat{a}_{\nu,{\bf k}}e^{i{\bf k}\cdot(\mathbf{l}+{\bf r}^{0}_{j})-i\omega_{\nu,{\bf k}}t}+\mathbf{e}^{\ast}_{\nu,j,{\bf k}}\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{\nu,{\bf k}}e^{-i{\bf k}\cdot(\mathbf{l}+{\bf r}^{0}_{j})+i\omega_{\nu,{\bf k}}t}\right) (106)

where the index ν\nu runs over all 3​n3n phonon modes and 𝐤{\bf k} is a regular, NN-point discretization of the first Brillouin zone. The 1/N1/\sqrt{N} factor implies that S⁡(𝐪,ω)S({\bf q},\omega) is an intrinsic quantity, as mentioned below (86). Inserting this in the two-point function, we can trivially perform the Wick contractions, at least in the zero temperature limit. (For the finite temperature result we refer to section 9.12 of [45].) This results in

⟨(𝐪⋅𝐮j′,0)​(0)​(𝐪⋅𝐮j,𝐥)​(t)⟩\displaystyle\langle({\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j^{\prime},0})(0)({\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j,{\bf l}})(t)\rangle =12​N​mj​mj′∑ν,𝐤1ων,𝐤(𝐪⋅𝐞ν,j′,𝐤)(𝐪⋅𝐞ν,j,𝐤∗)ei​ων,𝐤​te−i𝐤⋅𝐥ei​𝐤⋅(𝐫j′0−𝐫j0).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2N\sqrt{m_{j}m_{j^{\prime}}}}\sum_{\nu,{\bf k}}\frac{1}{\omega_{\nu,{\bf k}}}({\bf q}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{\nu,j^{\prime},{\bf k}})({\bf q}\cdot\mathbf{e}^{\ast}_{\nu,j,{\bf k}})e^{i\omega_{\nu,{\bf k}}t}e^{-i{\bf k}\cdot\mathbf{l}}e^{i{\bf k}\cdot({\bf r}_{j^{\prime}}^{0}-{\bf r}_{j}^{0})}. (107)

The Debye-Waller function is just the special case where j=j′j=j^{\prime}, 𝐥=0\mathbf{l}=0 and t=0t=0:

Wj​(𝐪)\displaystyle W_{j}({\bf q}) =12​⟨(𝐪⋅𝐮j,0)2⟩=14​N​mj​∑ν,𝐤1ων,𝐤​|𝐪⋅𝐞ν,j,𝐤|2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\langle({\bf q}\cdot{\bf u}_{j,0})^{2}\rangle=\frac{1}{4Nm_{j}}\sum_{\nu,{\bf k}}\frac{1}{\omega_{\nu,{\bf k}}}|{\bf q}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{\nu,j,{\bf k}}|^{2} (108)

Putting everything back together, we find

S⁡(𝐪,ω)=\displaystyle S({\bf q},\omega)= 12​N​∑j,j′,𝐥Aj​Aj′​ei​𝐪⋅(𝐫j0−𝐫j′0)​ei​𝐪⋅𝐥​e−Wj​(𝐪)​e−Wj′​(𝐪)​1mj​mj′\displaystyle\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{j,j^{\prime},{\bf l}}A_{j}A_{j^{\prime}}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot({\bf r}^{0}_{j}-{\bf r}^{0}_{j^{\prime}})}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot\mathbf{l}}e^{-W_{j}({\bf q})}e^{-W_{j^{\prime}}({\bf q})}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m_{j}m_{j^{\prime}}}} (109)
×∑ν3​n∑𝐤1ων,𝐤(𝐪⋅𝐞ν,j′,𝐤)(𝐪⋅𝐞ν,j,𝐤∗)e−i𝐤⋅𝐥ei​𝐤⋅(𝐫j′0−𝐫j0)δ(ων,𝐤−ω)\displaystyle\times\sum_{\nu}^{3n}\sum_{{\bf k}}\frac{1}{\omega_{\nu,{\bf k}}}({\bf q}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{\nu,j^{\prime},{\bf k}})({\bf q}\cdot\mathbf{e}^{\ast}_{\nu,j,{\bf k}})e^{-i{\bf k}\cdot\mathbf{l}}e^{i{\bf k}\cdot({\bf r}_{j^{\prime}}^{0}-{\bf r}_{j}^{0})}\delta(\omega_{\nu,{\bf k}}-\omega) (110)

where we used ∫−∞+∞d​t​ei⁡(ων,𝐤−ω)​t=2​π​δ​(ων,𝐤−ω)\int^{+\infty}_{-\infty}\!\!dt\,e^{i(\omega_{\nu,{\bf k}}-\omega)t}=2\pi\delta(\omega_{\nu,{\bf k}}-\omega). With the identity ∑𝐥ei​𝐪⋅𝐥=N​∑𝐆δ𝐪,𝐆\sum_{\mathbf{l}}e^{i{\bf q}\cdot\mathbf{l}}=N\sum_{\mathbf{G}}\delta_{{\bf q},{\bf G}} with 𝐆\mathbf{G} the reciprocal lattice vectors, this finally reduces to

S⁡(𝐪,ω)=12​∑𝐆,𝐤,ν1ων,𝐤​|Fν​(𝐪,𝐤)|2​δ𝐤−𝐪,𝐆​δ​(ων,𝐤−ω)S({\bf q},\omega)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\bf G},{\bf k},\nu}\frac{1}{\omega_{\nu,{\bf k}}}\left|F_{\nu}({\bf q},{\bf k})\right|^{2}\delta_{{\bf k}-{\bf q},{\bf G}}\delta(\omega_{\nu,{\bf k}}-\omega) (111)

with the phonon form factor

Fν​(𝐪,𝐤)≡∑jAjmj​e−Wj​(𝐪)​𝐪⋅𝐞ν,j,𝐤​ei⁡(𝐪−𝐤)⋅𝐫j0F_{\nu}({\bf q},{\bf k})\equiv\sum_{j}\frac{A_{j}}{\sqrt{m_{j}}}e^{-W_{j}({\bf q})}{\bf q}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{\nu,j,{\bf k}}e^{i({\bf q}-{\bf k})\cdot{\bf r}^{0}_{j}} (112)

Both energy and crystal momentum conservation are now manifest in these expressions. For scattering with sub-MeV dark matter, the momentum transfer is typically smaller than the size of the Brillouin zone, such that we can neglect the sum over the reciprocal lattice vectors and set 𝐆=0{\bf G}=0. In this limit, the structure factor further simplifies to

Slow​(𝐪,ω)≈12​∑ν1ων,𝐪​|Fνlow​(𝐪)|2​δ​(ων,𝐤−ω)S^{\text{low}}({\bf q},\omega)\approx\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\nu}\frac{1}{\omega_{\nu,{\bf q}}}\left|F^{\text{low}}_{\nu}({\bf q})\right|^{2}\delta(\omega_{\nu,{\bf k}}-\omega) (113)

with

Fνlow​(𝐪)≡∑jAjmj​e−Wj​(𝐪)​𝐪⋅𝐞ν,j,𝐪.F^{\text{low}}_{\nu}({\bf q})\equiv\sum_{j}\frac{A_{j}}{\sqrt{m_{j}}}e^{-W_{j}({\bf q})}{\bf q}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{\nu,j,{\bf q}}. (114)

Note that this expression differs from the one in [34] by a phase factor, since a different convention was used for the phonon eigenvectors.

Appendix D DM-electron scattering

In this appendix we comment on the reach for models where the DM couples to electrons through a scalar mediator. Such models tend to be extremely constrained by stellar cooling and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis bounds for mX≲1m_{X}\lesssim 1 MeV [80, 51], and at the moment we are not aware of models which can achieve σ¯e≳10−45​cm2\bar{\sigma}_{e}\gtrsim 10^{-45}\,\text{cm}^{2}. While it is likely difficult for near future experiments to access such low cross sections, we briefly discuss the reach for the sake of completeness.

Because the displacements involved in a phonon excitation correspond to displacements of the nucleus and tightly-bound inner shell electrons, a DM-electron coupling also results in an effective DM-phonon coupling, analogous to the discussion in Sec. IV for DM-nucleon couplings. The difference is that we must replace the mass number of the atom in the form factor (40) with the number of core electrons for each atom. Ga and As both have 28 core electrons, while O and Al have 2 and 10 core electrons, respectively.1111 11 As matter of convention we treat fully-filled shells as core electrons, explicitly this designates Al: 1​s21s^{2}, 2​s22s^{2}, 2​p62p^{6}, O: 1​s21s^{2}, Ga: 1​s21s^{2}, 2​s22s^{2}, 2​p62p^{6}, 3​s23s^{2}, 3​p63p^{6}, 3​d103d^{10} and As: 1​s21s^{2}, 2​s22s^{2}, 2​p62p^{6}, 3​s23s^{2}, 3​p63p^{6}, 3​d103d^{10} as core electrons. Note that the form factors for coherently scattering off the electrons in the atom are constant for |𝐪|≲1|{\bf q}|\lesssim 1 keV [81], and we can neglect their effect for the DM mass range of interest. For higher DM masses, these form factors are expected to suppress the rate.

The results are shown in Fig. 15 for a massless scalar mediator for a kg×\timesyear exposure, where we plot

σ¯e≡ye2​yX24​π​μe​X2(α​me)4,\bar{\sigma}_{e}\equiv\frac{y_{e}^{2}y_{X}^{2}}{4\pi}\frac{\mu_{eX}^{2}}{(\alpha m_{e})^{4}}, (115)

where yey_{e} (yXy_{X}) is the electron-mediator (DM-mediator) coupling, μe​X\mu_{eX} is the DM-electron reduced mass, and α\alpha is the fine structure constant. If only the optical branches are accessible, we find a reach that is competitive with that of Dirac material targets, in which the DM can create an electron excitation with ∼\sim meV threshold. In the optimistic case where the acoustic modes can also be resolved, polar materials could have a reach approaching that of a superconducting target.

Appendix E Statistical power of daily modulation signal

To estimate the discriminating power of the daily modulation, we calculate how many events are needed to distinguish the scenarios where (i) all observed events are due to a hypothetical, non-modulating background and (ii) all events are due to a modulating signal, as predicted in Sec. III.

For a given mass point mXm_{X} and an expected number of events NevN_{\text{ev}}, we generate simulated datasets for both scenarios above. The number of events in each dataset is Poisson distributed with average NevN_{\text{ev}}, and for the modulating sample the probability distribution in tt is given by the computations in Sec. III. For each dataset, we then perform a fit to the modulation, allowing for both a constant component and a modulating component with amplitude AA, fixing the template for that mXm_{X}. Denote the modulation amplitude as Anon-modA^{\text{non-mod}} for the datasets that are purely background, and AmodA^{\text{mod}} for the datasets that are purely signal. Repeating this procedure for many datasets, we generate the expected distribution in the modulation amplitude, shown in Fig. 17 for an example set of parameters. By construction, ⟨Amod⟩=1\langle A^{\text{mod}}\rangle=1, and ⟨Anod-mod⟩=0\langle A^{\text{nod-mod}}\rangle=0.

For each NevN_{\text{ev}}, we then compute the 2σ\sigma upper value (95% quantile) on AA for the non-modulating data (A2​σnon-modA^{\text{non-mod}}_{2\sigma}, indicated by the green arrow in Fig. 17). Interpolating in NevN_{\text{ev}}, we can then find the number of events needed such that A2​σnon-modA^{\text{non-mod}}_{2\sigma} is below the expected amplitude for the modulating sample, in other words A2​σnon-mod<1A^{\text{non-mod}}_{2\sigma}<1. This gives the number of events needed so that in 50% of the purely signal datasets, we can reject the background hypothesis at 2σ\sigma.

Similarly, we can obtain ±σ\pm\sigma quantiles about the mean expectation for the modulating signal (A±σmodA^{\text{mod}}_{\pm\sigma}, indicated by the blue arrows in Fig. 17). The ±σ\pm\sigma bands are then obtained by demanding that A2​σnon-mod<A±σmodA^{\text{non-mod}}_{2\sigma}<A^{\text{mod}}_{\pm\sigma}. The results of this procedure are shown in Fig. 17 as a function of mXm_{X}, and translated in terms of cross section in Fig. 5 (blue shaded band).

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
